Largest hot desert in the world, spanning North Africa. With an area of 9,200,000 sq km, it is the third-largest desert overall, smaller only than the deserts of Antarctica and the northern Arctic. It extends from the [[Red Sea]] in the east and the [[Mediterranean Sea]] in the north to the [[Atlantic Ocean]] in the west, and is bounded on the south by the [[Sahel]], a belt of semi-arid tropical savanna. It covers large parts of Algeria, Chad, Egypt, Libya, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Western Sahara, and Sudan, and parts of southern Morocco and Tunisia. Including all areas with a mean annual precipitation below 250 mm would enlarge it to 11 million sq km.

The terrain is diverse: rocky plateaus (hamada), sand seas (ergs) with dunes rising over 180 m, gravel plains (reg), dry valleys (wadi), dry lakes, and salt flats (shatt or chott). Mountain massifs, many volcanic, include the Aïr, Ahaggar, and Tibesti ranges; the highest peak is Emi Koussi, a shield volcano in the Tibesti of northern Chad. Important towns include [[Nouakchott]] and [[Timbuktu]].

The desert lies under the subtropical ridge, a belt of high pressure whose descending dry air prevents cloud formation and produces a hot desert climate ([[Köppen climate classification]] BWh). The Libyan Desert is the sunniest and driest part, rivaling the Atacama Desert. Summer highs often exceed 50 °C. For several hundred thousand years the region has alternated between desert and savanna in a 20,000-year cycle, driven by the precession of Earth's axis (about 26,000 years), which shifts the North African [[Monsoon|monsoon]].

Population is sparse, estimated at around 2.5 million, mostly nomadic pastoralists such as the Tuareg and Berbers and settlers near oases. The name derives from the Arabic *ṣaḥrā'*, "desert."

Mineral composed primarily of [[Sodium chloride|sodium chloride]] (NaCl), used as a seasoning and preservative. Granulated for food it is called table salt; as a natural crystalline mineral it is rock salt or halite. It is the source of the essential dietary minerals sodium and chlorine, and saltiness is one of the basic human tastes. Salting, brining, and pickling are ancient methods of [[Food preservation|food preservation]].

Some of the earliest evidence of salt processing, around 6000 BC, comes from present-day Romania, where people boiled spring water to extract salts; the harvest of salt from Xiechi Lake near Yuncheng, China, dates to at least 6000 BC. The mine at Solnitsata, Bulgaria, supplied the Balkans with salt from 5400 BC. Salt was prized by the ancient Hebrews, Greeks, Romans, Byzantines, Hittites, Egyptians, and Indians, who valued it highly as a trading commodity. It was carried by boat across the [[Mediterranean Sea]], along specially built salt roads, and across the [[Sahara]] by camel caravan; [[Herodotus]] described salt routes across Libya in the 5th century BC. The ancient Hebrews made a "covenant of salt" with God. Scarcity and universal need led nations to fight over salt and tax it, as in the El Paso Salt War of the late 1860s.

Salt is obtained from salt mines and by evaporating seawater and mineral-rich spring water in shallow pools. Of an annual global production of around three hundred million tonnes, only a small percentage is eaten; the greatest use is as a feedstock for chemicals such as caustic soda and chlorine, and for products such as polyvinyl chloride, plastics, and paper pulp. Table salt usually contains an anti-caking agent and may be [[Iodine|iodised]] to prevent iodine deficiency.

Sodium is essential to health as an electrolyte, but excessive salt consumption increases the risk of cardiovascular diseases such as [[Hypertension|hypertension]]. The [[World Health Organization]] recommends that adults consume less than 2,000 mg of sodium, equivalent to 5 grams of salt, per day.

Chemical compound consisting of an assembly of positively charged [[Ion|ions]] (cations) and negatively charged ions (anions), giving a compound with no net electric charge. The ions are held together by electrostatic forces termed [[Ionic bonding|ionic bonds]]. Also called an ionic compound, a salt may contain inorganic ions, such as chloride (Cl⁻), or organic ones, such as acetate (CH₃COO⁻), and ions that are monatomic, such as Na⁺, or polyatomic, such as ammonium (NH₄⁺) and carbonate (CO₃²⁻). Salts containing hydroxide (OH⁻) or oxide (O²⁻) ions are classified as bases.

Individual ions usually have several near neighbors, so they form part of a continuous three-dimensional network rather than molecules, and salts usually form [[Crystal|crystalline]] structures when solid. Salts of small ions typically have high melting and boiling points and are hard and brittle. As solids they are almost always electrical insulators, but when melted or dissolved they conduct well because the ions become mobile. Historically, the term referred only to the compound formed by neutralization of an acid and a base; as the definitions of acid and base broadened, it became synonymous with ionic compound, though the older distinction persists in some literature.

In 1913 William Henry Bragg and his son William Lawrence Bragg determined the structure of [[Sodium chloride|sodium chloride]], showing six equidistant nearest neighbors for each atom and a network with long-range crystalline order. Proof that such compounds are made of ions came in the mid-1920s from X-ray reflection experiments. [[Max Born]], Fritz Haber, and others developed the theory of ionic crystals; Born's predicted crystal energies matched thermochemical measurements.

Salts form when metals react with halogen gases, when solvent evaporates from a solution, or by precipitation on mixing two solutions. An [[Acid–base reaction|acid–base reaction]] gives a salt and water, for example NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. Salts formed from water solutions often include water of crystallization, forming hydrates.

Public health conditions related to clean drinking water and the treatment and disposal of human excreta and sewage. Sanitation systems aim to protect health by keeping people from contact with feces and stopping disease transmission, especially by the fecal–oral route. Adequate sanitation reduces [[Diarrhea|diarrhea]], a main cause of malnutrition and stunted growth in children, as well as ascariasis, [[Cholera|cholera]], hepatitis, polio, schistosomiasis, and trachoma.

Definitions vary. The [[World Health Organization]] defines it as the provision of facilities and services for the safe disposal of human urine and feces, together with the maintenance of hygienic conditions through services such as garbage collection and wastewater disposal. Many in the water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) sector include only excreta management. A sanitation system covers the capture, storage, transportation, treatment, and disposal or reuse of excreta and wastewater; the people who clean, maintain, operate, or empty its technologies are called sanitation workers. Approaches include community-led total sanitation, container-based sanitation, ecological sanitation, emergency sanitation, and onsite sanitation.

The purposes are a healthy living environment for everyone, protection of natural resources such as surface water, groundwater, and soil, and safety and dignity for people when they defecate or urinate. The human right to water and sanitation was recognized by the [[United Nations]] General Assembly in 2010, and sanitation is the subject of Sustainable Development Goal 6.

The Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) sanitation ladder, defined in 2016, begins at open defecation and rises through "unimproved," "limited," and "basic" to "safely managed." A 2017 JMP estimate found 4.5 billion people without safely managed sanitation. Later figures indicate that 1.2 billion people gained safely managed services between 2015 and 2024, raising coverage from 48% to 58%, while 3.4 billion still lack them, 354 million practice open defecation, and 432,000 deaths a year are attributed to inadequate sanitation, mostly in low- and middle-income countries. Lack of access affects [[Public health|public health]] as well as human dignity and personal safety.

Classical language of the Indo-Aryan branch of the [[Indo-European languages]], arising in South Asia in the late Bronze Age. It is the sacred language of [[Hinduism]], the language of classical Hindu philosophy, and of historical texts of [[Buddhism]] and Jainism. It served as a link language in ancient and medieval South Asia and, as Hindu and Buddhist culture spread, became a language of religion, high culture, and political elites in [[Southeast Asia]], East Asia, and Central Asia, leaving a lasting mark on their formal and learned vocabularies.

The most archaic form is Vedic Sanskrit, found in the Rigveda, a collection of 1,028 hymns composed between 1500 and 1200 BC by Indo-Aryan tribes migrating east from what is now northern Afghanistan. The [[Dravidian languages]] influenced its phonology and syntax. Classical Sanskrit, a refined and standardized form that emerged in the mid-1st millennium BC, was codified in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* ('Eight chapters') of [[Pāṇini]]. The dramatist Kālidāsa wrote in it, and the foundations of modern arithmetic were first described in it. The epics *Mahābhārata* and *Rāmāyaṇa* were composed in Epic Sanskrit, used in northern India between 400 BC and AD 300. Afterward Sanskrit stopped being learned as a first language and ceased developing as a living language.

The Rigveda was transmitted orally by memorization of exceptional rigor and fidelity, so its preserved syntax and morphology are vital to reconstructing Proto-Indo-European. Sanskrit has no attested native script; from around the turn of the 1st millennium AD it has been written in various [[Brahmic scripts]], most commonly in [[Devanagari]] today.

The name comes from *sáṃskṛta-*, a compound of *sáṃ* ('together, good, well, perfected') and *kṛta-* ('made, formed'), connoting a work "well prepared, pure and perfect, polished, sacred." Sanskrit is among the languages of the Eighth Schedule of India's Constitution. Although several thousand citizens have reported it as their mother tongue in recent censuses, there are no first-language speakers, and it remains a ceremonial and ritual language. The oldest Sanskrit college is the Benares Sanskrit College, founded in 1791.

Object, typically a [[Spacecraft|spacecraft]], placed into [[Orbit|orbit]] around a celestial body. Satellites serve for communication relay, weather forecasting, navigation, broadcasting, scientific research, and Earth observation; military uses include reconnaissance, early warning, and signals intelligence. Defunct satellites and the final rocket stages that place satellites in orbit are also counted.

Except for passive satellites, most generate electricity with solar panels or radioisotope thermoelectric generators, and most carry transponders for communication with ground stations. Many use a standardized bus, the most popular being small CubeSats, and similar satellites can work together as constellations. A spacecraft becomes a satellite by reaching orbital velocity in an orbit high enough to avoid decay from atmospheric drag and above its Roche limit; propulsion, usually chemical or ion thrusters, can then change or maintain the orbit. As of 2018, about 90% of satellites orbiting Earth were in [[Low Earth orbit]] or [[Geostationary orbit|geostationary orbit]], where a satellite stays fixed relative to a point on the ground. Some imaging satellites use a Sun-synchronous orbit to scan the globe under similar lighting. Space telescopes exploit the near-perfect vacuum of space to observe across the electromagnetic spectrum.

The first published mathematical study of an artificial satellite was Newton's cannonball, a thought experiment by [[Isaac Newton]] in 1687. Edward Everett Hale's story "The Brick Moon" (1869) was the first fictional depiction of a launch into orbit. In 1903 Konstantin Tsiolkovsky published the first academic treatise on using rocketry to launch spacecraft, and Herman Potočnik described geostationary satellites in 1928. In 1945 [[Arthur C. Clarke]] described how three geostationary satellites could cover the entire planet with communications, and in 1946 Lyman Spitzer proposed an orbiting space telescope.

The first artificial satellite was the Soviet Union's [[Sputnik 1]], launched October 4, 1957, followed by the U.S. *Explorer 1* in 1958. As of June 28, 2025, 12,952 satellites orbited Earth: 8,530 belonging to the United States, 1,559 to Russia, and 908 to China. Growing numbers of satellites and debris raise the threat of collision, including the possibility of a debris cascade known as Kessler syndrome.

Sixth planet from the Sun and second largest in the Solar System, after Jupiter. A [[Gas giant|gas giant]] with an average radius about 9 times that of Earth, it has an eighth of Earth's average density but is over 95 times more massive. It orbits the Sun at 9.59 AU (1,434 million km) in 29.45 years. Visible features rotate at different rates by latitude, with a day of about 10.7 hours.

Saturn is composed predominantly of hydrogen and helium and lacks a definite surface. Its interior is thought to include a diffuse rocky and icy core, a deep layer of [[Metallic hydrogen|metallic hydrogen]], a layer of liquid hydrogen and helium, and an outer gas layer. A 2004 estimate put the core at 9–22 times Earth's mass. Its average density, 0.69 g/cm³, makes it the only planet less dense than water. It radiates 2.5 times more energy than it receives from the Sun, possibly in part through the "raining out" of helium droplets in its interior. Ammonia crystals in the upper atmosphere give it a pale yellow hue, and winds reach 1,800 km/h. A persistent hexagonal pattern surrounds the north pole. Its magnetic field is weaker than Earth's at the surface but has a magnetic moment 580 times as great.

The [[Ring system|rings]] are bright and extensive, composed mainly of water ice with a smaller amount of rocky debris and dust. The main system spans about 282,000 km, with divisions such as the 4,700-km-wide Cassini Division. At least 293 moons orbit Saturn, 63 of them officially named. [[Titan (moon)|Titan]], the largest, is the second largest moon in the Solar System, larger than Mercury, and the only moon with a substantial atmosphere. [[Enceladus]] ejects water plumes that point to a subsurface ocean.

NASA's Pioneer 11 flew past in 1979, followed by [[Voyager 1]] and Voyager 2 in the early 1980s and the Cassini–Huygens mission from 2004 to 2017, which landed the Huygens probe on Titan. The planet is named for the Roman god of wealth and agriculture, father of Jupiter; Saturday is "Saturn's Day."

Kingdom, West Asia, occupying the bulk of the [[Arabian Peninsula]] (pop., 2024: 36,544,431). Its land area of about 2,149,690 sq km makes it the fifth-largest country in Asia and the twelfth-largest in the world. It is bordered by the Red Sea to the west, Jordan, Iraq, and Kuwait to the north, the Persian Gulf, Bahrain, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates to the east, Oman to the southeast, and Yemen to the south. [[Riyadh]] is the capital and largest city; other major centers include Jeddah and the two holiest cities in Islam, [[Mecca]] and [[Medina]].

The territory was the site of several ancient cultures, and archaeological study has identified some of the earliest traces of human activity outside Africa. Islam emerged there in the early 7th century, and after the death of Muhammad in 632 his followers expanded Muslim rule into North Africa, Central and South Asia, and Iberia. Arab dynasties from the region founded the Rashidun (632–661), Umayyad (661–750), and Abbasid (750–1258) caliphates, among others.

The modern state was founded in 1932 by King Abdulaziz, who united Hejaz, Najd, and parts of Eastern and South Arabia through campaigns beginning in 1902. It is the Third Saudi State, successor to the First (1727–1818) and Second (1824–1891). It is an absolute monarchy under the [[House of Saud]], with Islam as official religion and Arabic as official language. The ultraconservative Wahhabi movement within Sunni Islam was the prevailing political and cultural force until the 2000s. Critics cite its intervention in the Yemeni civil war, restrictions on political and civil liberties, and human rights record; since the mid-2010s the government has introduced limited, gradual social, cultural, and religious reforms, including the Vision 2030 economic diversification program associated with Crown Prince [[Mohammed bin Salman]].

Since [[Petroleum|petroleum]] was discovered in 1938, the kingdom has become the world's second-largest oil producer and leading exporter, with the second-largest oil reserves. A founding member of [[OPEC]], the UN, and the Arab League, it is the only Arab member of the G20 and the largest economy in the Middle East. Foreign-born residents make up roughly 40% of the population, and about half of Saudis are under 25.

Institution designed to provide learning environments for the teaching of students, usually under the direction of teachers. Most countries have formal [[Education|education]] systems, sometimes compulsory, in which students progress through a series of government or private schools. These generally include primary school for young children and secondary school for teenagers; higher education is commonly taught at a university or college. Kindergarten or preschool serve children aged about 3–5, and vocational schools, seminaries, and schools for adult training are also found. Private schools may be religious, such as the gurukula (Hindu), madrasa (Arabic), hawza (Shi'i Muslim), and yeshiva (Jewish), or may emphasize higher standards. Homeschooling and distance education take place outside the school building.

The word derives from Greek *scholē*, originally "leisure" and later "a group to whom lectures were given." Formal schools have existed at least since ancient Greece, Rome, India, and China. The Byzantine Empire had a schooling system beginning at the primary level, which continued until 1453. In Western Europe cathedral schools were founded in the early Middle Ages to teach future clergy and administrators; the oldest still operating include The King's School, Canterbury (established AD 597). Monastic schools taught religious and secular subjects from the 5th century. Universities emerged in the 12th century. During the Middle Ages and much of the early modern period, the main purpose of schools was to teach Latin, giving rise to the term "grammar school." The curriculum gradually broadened to include vernacular literacy and technical, artistic, and scientific subjects. In the Islamic world, mosques at first combined worship and learning, but by the 9th century the madrasa, an institution independent of any mosque, had appeared. Obligatory attendance became common in parts of Europe in the 18th century; Denmark-Norway introduced it in 1739–41.

Proponents regard schools as effective means of education. Critics argue that they fail to prepare students for adult life, favor certain temperaments over others, prescribe what students do and when, and, through grades and homework, inhibit natural curiosity and creativity. Compulsory attendance now lasts from 9 to 13 years in nearly all countries, yet approximately 250 million children remain out of school.

Systematic discipline that builds and organizes knowledge in the form of testable explanations about nature and society. It is driven by the [[Scientific method|scientific method]], an empirical cycle that typically involves making observations, producing hypotheses, testing them with evidence, and drawing conclusions. Science encompasses both this process and the body of knowledge it produces, which the scientific community continuously challenges, validates, and organizes. Its claims are expected to be testable, replicable, and falsifiable, which distinguishes them from anecdotal assertion.

Modern science is typically divided into two major branches: the [[Natural science|natural sciences]], which study the physical world, and the [[Social science|social sciences]], which study individuals and societies. Logic, mathematics, and theoretical computer science, sometimes called the formal sciences, are typically regarded as separate because they rely on deductive reasoning rather than the scientific method. Applied sciences, such as engineering and medicine, use scientific knowledge for practical purposes.

The word has been used in English since the 14th century in the sense of "the state of knowing," borrowed from Anglo-Norman and ultimately from Latin *scientia*, 'knowledge, awareness, understanding.' Scientists were once called "natural philosophers" or "men of science"; in 1834 William Whewell introduced the term *scientist*, crediting it to "some ingenious gentleman," possibly himself.

Science has no single origin; scientific thinking emerged gradually over tens of thousands of years in different forms around the world. Direct evidence becomes clearer with the writing systems of the Bronze Age civilizations of Egypt and Mesopotamia (c. 3000–1200 BC), whose contributions to mathematics, astronomy, and medicine later entered Greek and medieval science. The Egyptians developed a non-positional decimal numbering system, solved practical problems with geometry, and devised a calendar. The Mesopotamians used knowledge of natural chemicals to manufacture pottery, glass, soap, and metals, and the earliest medical prescriptions appear in Sumerian.

In classical antiquity there was no real analogue of the modern scientist; educated, usually upper-class men investigated nature as time allowed. The Milesian school, founded by [[Thales of Miletus]] and continued by Anaximander and Anaximenes, first attempted to explain natural phenomena without relying on the supernatural. Leucippus and his student Democritus developed the theory of atoms, and Epicurus later built a full natural cosmology on atomism. Hippocrates established the tradition of systematic medical science. Greek [[Natural philosophy|natural philosophy]] was shaped by earlier Near Eastern work and by later medieval scholarship, with further advances, including the Hindu–Arabic numeral system, made during the Golden Age of India and the [[Islamic Golden Age]].

The recovery of Greek works and Islamic inquiries in Western Europe during the Renaissance revived natural philosophy, which the [[Scientific Revolution]], beginning in the 16th century, transformed as new ideas departed from Greek conceptions. In the 19th century the institutional and professional features of science took shape, and "natural philosophy" gave way to "natural science." Contemporary research is often collaborative, carried out by teams in universities, research institutions, government agencies, and companies, though major advances are also credited to individuals and recognized through awards such as the [[Nobel Prize]]. Science policy seeks to guide the responsible development of commercial products, health care, public infrastructure, environmental protection, and defense. The replication crisis, in which results in fields such as psychology and biomedicine have repeatedly failed to reproduce, has prompted calls for preregistration and open data.
